scenarios.title: Share a public address and recover replies
scenarios.summary: Share one public address while returning tracked replies and blocking new inbound traffic.
scenarios.objective: Allow NEW traffic from LAN 10.20.30.0/24 on lan0, leaving wan0, only to 203.0.113.9 using TCP destination port 443. Keep ESTABLISHED traffic passing in the supplied topology. Refuse other NEW traffic, including new inbound requests and UDP impostors. Translate the required outbound source to public address 198.51.100.1. Clients 10.20.30.55 and 10.20.30.56 both use source port 40000; they need distinct usable public mappings and replies to the correct private client. Keep PREROUTING, INPUT, OUTPUT and the supplied route/interface facts unchanged. Equivalent supported FORWARD and source-translation rules are accepted.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Inspect the failed policy or traffic event. Compare expected and actual addresses, state and port; change one cause and retry. Unsupported commands keep the previous configuration and explain the supported subset.

Verify the complete policy and sample traffic

guide.title: Inspect both rule sets
guide.why: A connection is identified by its protocol and both address/port pairs. 172.20.4.55:41000 means address 172.20.4.55 using port 41000. Two clients can choose the same source port because their private addresses differ. TCP and UDP remain different conversations.
guide.action: Choose iptables -S and iptables -t nat -S from Example command; Insert command only fills the field, then Run command applies it.

commands.explanation: Inspect the current example filter before changing it; this query applies nothing.
Inspect the example PREROUTING and POSTROUTING rules and their order.

guide.title: Repair and observe two clients
guide.why: NEW means this tracked conversation has not been seen in both directions. The first observed reply is ESTABLISHED; this does not prove a complete TCP handshake or working application. An ESTABLISHED permit lets tracked traffic return without permitting an unrelated NEW arrival.
guide.action: Use the complete worked commands if needed. Select Two clients share one address and Run traffic test. Use Inspect event to compare the second request and both replies.

commands.explanation: Clear the example’s obsolete FORWARD entries; this retains the chain policy.
Use DROP when no required permit matches.
Permit tracked traffic that has been observed in both directions; this is not an unsolicited NEW permit.

commands.command: iptables -A FORWARD -i lan0 -o wan0 -s 172.20.4.0/24 -d 198.51.100.9 -p tcp --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j ACCEPT
commands.explanation: Permit only the example LAN’s new TCP web requests toward its stated remote server.
Remove the obsolete source rule so it cannot shadow its replacement.

commands.command: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o wan0 -s 172.20.4.0/24 -p tcp -j SNAT --to-source 192.0.2.1
commands.explanation: Use the example public source address. With no explicit port range, preserve a free port or allocate another in its modeled class.

guide.title: Check, then diagnose a new mistake
guide.why: Source NAT (SNAT) replaces the outgoing source address after the FORWARD filter. The router retains a mapping so replies return to the right client. If two clients would produce the same public tuple, they need different translated source ports. NAT alone does not allow traffic through the filter.
guide.action: Choose Check example. Try the one-port rule from the command picker, run the traffic test and check again; remove that inserted first POSTROUTING rule and retry.

commands.command: iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING 1 -s 172.20.4.0/24 -o wan0 -p tcp -j SNAT --to-source 192.0.2.1:41000
commands.explanation: Intentional mistake: this first source rule has only one public port for two equal-port client requests.
Remove only the first rule inserted during the deliberate mistake exercise.

scenarios.explanation: NEW and ESTABLISHED serve different purposes: allow the stated new web requests and let observed tracked traffic return while other new requests stay blocked. Source translation gives the required LAN traffic the supplied public address; distinct public ports separate the two clients using the same private source port. The mapping restores each reply’s private destination. The exact prefix/state checks prevent a solution restricted to only the displayed clients. These are bounded header/connection trials, not proof of TCP or application completion.
hints: A connection is identified by its protocol and both address/port pairs. 172.20.4.55:41000 means address 172.20.4.55 using port 41000. Two clients can choose the same source port because their private addresses differ. TCP and UDP remain different conversations.

NEW means this tracked conversation has not been seen in both directions. The first observed reply is ESTABLISHED; this does not prove a complete TCP handshake or working application. An ESTABLISHED permit lets tracked traffic return without permitting an unrelated NEW arrival.

Source NAT (SNAT) replaces the outgoing source address after the FORWARD filter. The router retains a mapping so replies return to the right client. If two clients would produce the same public tuple, they need different translated source ports. NAT alone does not allow traffic through the filter.
scenarios.simplifications: Supplied two-interface numeric IPv4 TCP/UDP normal-flow profile only. NEW/ESTABLISHED and DNAT flags are not a complete TCP stack or application test. Each traffic trial uses new sample flows and an empty simulated connection table; rules and drafts are retained. The native traffic controls are simulator actions, not Linux commands. No host networking, kernel/service/file changes, raw packets, ICMP/RELATED/INVALID, IPv6, timers, helpers or OUTPUT/local/hairpin NAT. Port allocation is bounded and deterministic, not the kernel algorithm. Mathematical proofs cover declared header/state and translation domains; unsupported complexity cannot pass. See docs/LINUX_CONNECTIONS_SUBSET.md; primary references checked 2026-11-14.

scenarios.title: Publish one service with a precise destination policy
scenarios.summary: Publish one public TCP endpoint without opening direct private-address access or breaking existing outbound traffic.
scenarios.objective: Publish only 198.51.100.1 TCP/8443 arriving on wan0, forwarding it to private server 10.20.30.42 TCP/443 on lan0. Permit that rewritten endpoint only when destination translation actually occurred. Refuse NEW requests sent directly to the private address; keep ESTABLISHED traffic passing. Leave other incoming destinations unchanged: no other public port, address or UDP endpoint is published by these rules. Preserve NEW LAN TCP/443 access to 203.0.113.9 and its public source translation to 198.51.100.1, including clients 10.20.30.55 and 10.20.30.56 using source port 40000 and their replies. Keep router-local INPUT/OUTPUT, routes and interfaces as supplied. Equivalent supported policy/translation rules are accepted.

guide.title: Find the address stage that is wrong
guide.why: Destination NAT (DNAT) changes the destination before route selection and FORWARD filtering. In this worked network, public 192.0.2.1:9443 becomes private server 172.20.4.42:443. The filter must match the rewritten private address and port, rather than the public tuple.
guide.action: Inspect filter and NAT rules, then select Reach the published service and Run traffic test. Inspect the first external request.

commands.explanation: Inspect the current example filter before changing it; this query applies nothing.
Inspect the example PREROUTING and POSTROUTING rules and their order.

guide.title: Repair the target and the permit
guide.why: The retained connection mapping reverses the destination change for replies. The external client therefore sees replies from 192.0.2.1:9443, not from the server’s private address. Source translation for unrelated outbound clients is a separate POSTROUTING rule set.
guide.action: Use the separate worked commands to correct PREROUTING and the FORWARD permit. Run the published-service, direct-private and outbound two-client tests.

commands.explanation: Clear the example’s obsolete FORWARD entries; this retains the chain policy.
Use DROP when no required permit matches.
Permit tracked traffic that has been observed in both directions; this is not an unsolicited NEW permit.

commands.command: iptables -A FORWARD -i lan0 -o wan0 -s 172.20.4.0/24 -d 198.51.100.9 -p tcp --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j ACCEPT
commands.explanation: Permit only the example LAN’s new TCP web requests toward its stated remote server.

commands.command: iptables -A FORWARD -i wan0 -o lan0 -d 172.20.4.42 -p tcp --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate DNAT -j ACCEPT
commands.explanation: Permit the rewritten example server endpoint only when destination translation actually happened.
Remove the wrong publishing target without clearing the separate source-translation rules.

commands.command: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i wan0 -d 192.0.2.1 -p tcp --dport 9443 -j DNAT --to-destination 172.20.4.42:443
commands.explanation: Rewrite only the example public TCP/9443 endpoint to private 172.20.4.42:443, before routing and filtering.

guide.title: Check the boundary, not only the server
guide.why: The conntrack DNAT flag says this connection’s destination was rewritten. It is independent of NEW/ESTABLISHED. A comma list means either condition: NEW,DNAT would also match a NEW request sent directly to the private server. Require DNAT for this inbound service permit and keep the separate ESTABLISHED permit.
guide.action: Choose Check example. Try the NEW,DNAT rule from the picker, then run Direct private address stays protected. Delete that inserted first FORWARD rule and retry.

commands.command: iptables -I FORWARD 1 -i wan0 -o lan0 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW,DNAT -j ACCEPT
commands.explanation: Intentional mistake: a comma list matches NEW OR DNAT, so it can admit a direct private request. Inspect the failing test before deleting it.
Remove only the first rule inserted during the deliberate mistake exercise.

scenarios.explanation: PREROUTING changes the public destination before routing and filtering. A FORWARD permit therefore uses the private server and port, and the independent DNAT flag prevents a directly addressed private request from borrowing that permit. ESTABLISHED keeps tracked traffic passing. The original mapping gives replies the public source endpoint. Destination-scope proofs reject extra redirects, while separate outbound cases ensure the source-translation path was preserved.
